questions.title: Auto-Expire Cache
questions.summary: Build a cache where entries become invisible after their time-to-live passes.
questions.prompt: Design a key-value cache that accepts a time-to-live for each write and returns no value after an item expires.
constraints: The clock is supplied by the caller in this MVP prompt.

diagrams.title: Expiry lifecycle
diagrams.mermaid:
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Fresh
  Fresh --> Expired: now >= expiresAt
  Expired --> Removed: cleanup or read

solutionTracks.title: Lazy Expiration Map
solutionTracks.summary: Store each value with its expiry time and remove expired entries only when a key is read or overwritten.

steps.title: Store expiry metadata
steps.explanation: Every set writes the value and the absolute time at which it should stop being visible.

steps.title: Check on get
steps.explanation: Reads compare the current time against the stored expiry before returning a value.

steps.title: Delete stale keys
steps.explanation: If the entry is expired, delete it and behave like the key was missing.

solutionTracks.explanation: The cache never returns stale data because every read validates the expiry timestamp. It avoids background cleanup work, trading memory cleanup latency for simpler operations.

solutionTracks.title: Min Heap Cleanup
solutionTracks.summary: Add a min heap ordered by expiry time so stale entries can be removed before reads or on a cleanup tick.

steps.title: Push expiry events
steps.explanation: Every write stores the value in a map and pushes expiry time plus key into a min heap.

steps.title: Clean oldest first
steps.explanation: Before operations, pop heap entries whose expiry time is not in the future.

steps.title: Ignore stale heap records
steps.explanation: If a key was overwritten, only delete it when the heap expiry matches the map expiry.

solutionTracks.explanation: The heap tells which entries can expire next, while the map holds the authoritative latest value. Matching expiry times prevents old heap records from deleting newer writes.

complexity.time: O(log n) set, amortized O(log n) cleanup

questions.title: Detect Cycle In A Dependency Graph
questions.summary: Determine whether directed service or job dependencies contain a cycle.
questions.prompt: Given a directed graph of dependencies, return true if there is a cycle and false if all dependencies can be ordered.

examples.input: A -> B, B -> C, C -> A
examples.explanation: The dependencies loop back to A.

diagrams.title: Cycle signal
diagrams.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A --> B
  B --> C
  C --> A

solutionTracks.title: DFS Coloring
solutionTracks.summary: Color every node as unvisited, visiting, or done to detect a back edge in a directed dependency graph.

steps.title: Mark visiting
steps.explanation: When DFS enters a node, mark it as currently on the recursion path.

steps.title: Detect back edges
steps.explanation: If DFS reaches a visiting node, the graph contains a cycle through the active path.

steps.title: Mark done
steps.explanation: After all outgoing edges are safe, mark the node done so future traversals can skip it.

solutionTracks.explanation: A dependency cycle exists exactly when a path reaches a node already on that same active path. The visiting color represents that active path without needing to copy it each time.

solutionTracks.title: Kahn Topological Count
solutionTracks.summary: Repeatedly remove nodes with zero incoming edges; remaining nodes imply a directed cycle.

steps.title: Count indegrees
steps.explanation: For every edge, increment the incoming edge count of the dependent node.

steps.title: Process ready nodes
steps.explanation: Start with every zero-indegree node and remove its outgoing edges from the graph.

steps.title: Compare processed count
steps.explanation: If fewer nodes are processed than exist, the unprocessed nodes are trapped in cycles.

solutionTracks.explanation: A directed acyclic graph always has at least one zero-indegree node in every remaining subgraph. If the process stalls early, every remaining node depends on another remaining node.

questions.title: Longest Distinct Viewing Window
questions.summary: Find the longest contiguous viewing sequence with no repeated title.
questions.prompt: Given an array of watched title identifiers, return the length of the longest contiguous window with no duplicate identifiers.

examples.explanation: B,C,A,D is the longest distinct window.

solutionTracks.title: Sliding Window Set
solutionTracks.summary: Maintain a window with no repeated titles by moving the left edge past duplicates as they appear.

steps.title: Expand right
steps.explanation: Add each next viewing item to the active window when it is not already present.

steps.title: Shrink on duplicate
steps.explanation: If the item is already inside the window, remove items from the left until the duplicate leaves.

steps.title: Record best length
steps.explanation: After each insertion, the window is distinct, so its length is a valid candidate.

solutionTracks.explanation: The window invariant is that every item inside it is unique. Each pointer moves only forward, so the scan stays linear while considering every maximal distinct window.

python.label: Python
python.code:
def longest_distinct(items):
    seen = set()
    left = 0
    best = 0
    for right, item in enumerate(items):
        while item in seen:
            seen.remove(items[left])
            left += 1
        seen.add(item)
        best = max(best, right - left + 1)
    return best

solutionTracks.title: Last Seen Index Jump
solutionTracks.summary: Remember the latest index of each title and jump the left edge directly when a duplicate appears.

steps.title: Store last indexes
steps.explanation: A map records the most recent position where each item appeared.

steps.title: Jump left safely
steps.explanation: When a duplicate is inside the current window, move left to one position after the previous occurrence.

steps.title: Update best
steps.explanation: The window between left and right is distinct after the jump, so update the maximum length.

solutionTracks.explanation: The left edge never moves backward. Jumping past the previous duplicate preserves uniqueness and avoids removing each intermediate item one by one.
